Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to say something if the hon. gentleman is finished.
The hon. member for Temiscouata seems to object to the form of the public accounts.
I wish to make a distinction clear. The statement of the public accounts is one document; the auditor general's report is another. The public accounts are published on October 31, the same day as that on which the auditor general's report must be issued. The public accounts are presented to the Minister of Finance by the deputy minister of finance, for issue and publication. The auditor general's report is tabled through the Minister of Finance. The deputy minister of finance is the permanent head of the Department of Finance; he is a civil servant, an official of the government, in the employ of the government. The auditor general on the other hand is an officer of this parliament and answerable to this parliament.
I have made inquiries as to the form of the public accounts. I find that the public
accounts are in the same form and practically of the same dimensions as they have been for a great many years. I think when hon. gentlemen talk about the public accounts, in many instances they have in mind the auditor general's report. That certainly was true of the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport this afternoon. He referred several times to the volume which he held in his hands, as the "public accounts." That volume was the auditor general's report. If hon. members of the house are criticizing the form of the auditor general's report, it is something they have a right to do. I think it is true that in the auditor general's report he does not give a detailed statement of individual expenditures of less than $25,000. I also believe it to be true that he does give a statement of civilian expenditures in greater detail. At the present time the question whether the form, the amount of detail, in both the public accounts and the auditor general's report should not be changed is under active consideration, and it may be that we can make changes which will be beneficial. It may be that parts of the material now published in the auditor general's report should be incorporated in the public accounts, to let the Minister of Finance take direct responsibility for it as head of the Department of Finance. That is under consideration at the present time, and a little later I think I may be able to make some recommendations to the house in that regard, which the house may debate if it wishes to do so. I do not mean within a week or so, or even within a few weeks, but I just want to tell the committee that this matter is under active consideration.
I do not want to say very much more about the speech of the hon. member for Temiscouata, but I do think I ought to say something about the deputy minister of finance. I do not need to do this for the sake of the general public or the great mass of people who deal with the Department of Finance. I am not saying this out of any sense of loyalty or sentiment, or anything like that; but if hon. members of this house are interested in my views I want to give it as my opinion that in respect of ability, in respect of character and in respect of devotion to duty I have never met anyone who ranked higher, and I have met very few who ranked as high. I want to say that about the deputy minister of finance. I have no personal knowledge as to the circumstances of his coming here, but I believe he was sought after, and almost anxiously sought after, because of his high reputation. I did not work with him, of course, when the previous
War Appropriation-Finanace

government was in. power, when the Bank of Canada was established, when the housing legislation was launched, or when any of those important measures-and they were important measures, which have proved beneficial during the course of the years-were gotten under way. I know that he had a great deal to do in assisting, and probably in suggesting, that those measures be undertaken. But in recent years, since the outbreak of war, both as acting Minister of Finance and as Minister of Finance, naturally I have worked in very close association with my deputy. We have gone through some very serious times; we have undertaken some very large and comprehensive measures. You cannot set up a great organization such as the national war finance committee, or the foreign exchange control board, or the wartime prices and trade board, without doing an enormous amount of work, when you must have good advice and when you must have with you a clear thinker, a hard worker and a patriotic citizen. The deputy minister of finance is all of that.
Consider some of the things that have been done by the Department of Finance-and I am not saying this to pat that department on the back but rather to give hon. members of the committee some idea of the magnitude of the work. In our financial arrangements with Britain we broke entirely new ground and did an unprecedented thing which I feel sure has the approval of this and other countries. We undertook a comprehensive programme of getting foreign exchange into this country and of conserving foreign exchange by making scores of agreements, some of them involving very large sums of money, under the War Exchange Conservation Act-a most trying kind of work; meeting individuals and companies from all over the dominion and making agreements with them for amortization, depreciation, and so on. We have been dealing with the provinces for the last year, negotiating agreements with them resulting in the provinces vacating the income and corporation tax fields, something in which a sister dominion is now attempting to follow us, as the United States followed us in regard to our price ceiling policy. You cannot do things like these without the help of a person who is a good man. I am willing to give some scope to hon. members of this house in what they say about civil servants, but in regard to this particular civil servant, even though it may not be strictly in order I feel that I owe it to him to state what I have stated, for what my opinion is worth.
I do not think any comment is necessary with regard to the other things mentioned by
[Mr. Ilsley.3
the hon. member for Temiscouata, such as the passage of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, and so on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
At this stage I should like to point out to hon. members paragraph 305 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, which states:
All references to judges and courts of justice and to personages of high official station, of the nature of personal attack and censure, have always been considered unparliamentary, and the Speakers of the British and Canadian houses have always treated them as breaches of order.
In the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata I did not find any direct attack, but certainly there were indirect insinuations affecting the character of these high officials. I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that attacks of this kind are out of order.

I do not propose to break the rules, Mr. Chairman, though I think some of the criticisms offered this afternoon by the hon. member for Temiscouata with regard to the public accounts were well taken. The public accounts committee should be functioning; there should be a thorough investigation by parliament of the expenditures made by the government. I do not think we are doing our duty in this parliament when we fail to examine the public accounts in committee. May I say, too, that if this procedure were followed I believe we would facilitate the business of this house. I think we all feel that the business of the house has been dragging along during the last couple of weeks in a way that is a reflection upon all of us, and I should like to see a speeding up of the business. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with your permission I am going to say everything I have to say on this matter at the present time.
I rose primarily this afternoon to speak of the staff in the auditor general's office and of the personnel under the civil service commission, which is covered in. the next item. I have been greatly alarmed by the influx of young people from western Canada into Ottawa, and the lack of accommodation for them. I have before me at this time-and I will not give the authority, although I shall be glad to give it to the minister-a report which has been prepared by a reputable social service organization in this city, outlining some of the conditions found here. The war has brought a very large number of people into this city. I suppose each one of us, irrespective of where he sits in the house, knows a number of young men and young girls who have come in from his own constituency, many of them from rural communities, and have found work in

War Appropriation-Finance
the various government departments under the civil service commission. Most hon. members know that the conditions under which many of these girls have to live at the present time are deplorable. For example, we hear about the high prices charged for board and room, about the overcrowding and even in some instances about the poor board these girls are getting.
I shall give only one or two examples of many I have before me. Let us first take the ease of three girls-and may I say that each one of these I am about to mention can be thoroughly substantiated. These three girls share a bedroom, and each pays $35 a month for room and board. The landlady is thus getting $105 a month for one room, and board for the three girls.
Disgraceful.

Another woman has a room for which she wants $55 a month, without meals, if one person occupies it. If two girls take it she will give them breakfast and evening dinner if they pay her $45 a month each. It will be realized at once that with the salaries paid in this city at the present time neither the auditor general's office nor the civil service generally can be doing other than exploiting these girls. I will not say the officials are exploiting them, but they are being exploited jointly by ourselves and by the landladies. In some instances girls are not permitted even to entertain friends in rooms for which they have paid these high prices. I repeat that these cases are authentic. Some girls have been taken to places which were not fit for girls to live in. Something needs to be done by the government immediately to cope with this situation in Ottawa. A few days ago I noticed in a local paper a report of a discussion in the local council. This newspaper, dated May 22, 1942-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member indicate to what item he refers?

I am talking about the stall of the auditor general's office, and about the personnel under the civil service commission, which is next. I was directing my remarks to the two items, but if you wish me to make two speeches, Mr. Chairman, I will do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item which comes next is "supply of personnel for war services." The hon. member is now discussing the housing accommodation for that personnel?

I am discussing the supply of personnel for war services, with special reference to the housing accommodation in this city for that personnel. And may
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, with all due respect, that unless these girls are provided with proper remuneration and proper accommodation we shall not be able to get girls to come to this city to form part of the personnel of the civil service. Therefore I suggest I am within the bounds of these items.
This matter has been before the council of the city of Ottawa. The city has made representations to the government asking that it provide accommodation for the lower paid female help, which is included in the personnel mentioned in the item. The reply from the Prime Minister to the approach by the controllers of the city was most unsatisfactory. This letter, from Mr. Henry, Mr. King's private secretary, states:
Mr. King wishes me to say that the government is not unmindful of the need in this respect, and has been giving a great deal of consideration to the matter. There are of course a number of circumstances which must be taken into consideration. One difficulty has been that some of the controllers of war-materials and building supplies have found it very difficult, if not impossible, to release certain supplies at this time which are required for war purposes.
Yet at the same council meeting it was reported that a brewers' warehouse is being erected on Catherine street, that a permit therefor has been issued, and that the necessary building materials had been released for the purpose. I submit if materials can be found for a brewers' warehouse we ought to be able to find materials to provide decent accommodation in Ottawa for our employees.
As I have said, many of the girls come from constituencies far away. Some come from my own constituency in western Canada,. I know that many of them are suffering in health, and the loss in days by the departments is really a reflection of the conditions under which they live. I am not going to give figures, but if the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Munitions and Supply will look into the health records in their departments they will find that an enormous number of days are being lost because of ill health among young girls working in Ottawa.
If we are to appropriate the large sum of money mentioned in the item to the supply of personnel for war services, and if we are bringing into this city girls from outside points, then it is our bounden duty to see to it that proper accommodation is afforded.
The same condition existed in Washington. In that city the government is erecting hostels for the girls. Under date line of May 12 a dispatch from Washington states that the girls working there for the government, who will live in a new federally-financed hostel for
War Appropriation-Finance

women, will pay $34.50 a mouth for a single room, without bath. However, they may entertain. That rate of course is too high for the girls employed in Ottawa under the present salary schedule.
And that is also without meals.

Yes. But it does show that in Washington, where they are paying higher salaries, some attempt is being made by the government to deal with a similar situation. When we look around the city and see huge temporary office buildings going up, we must realize that if we are going to bring people to this city to work in government offices we ought to make provision whereby they may have decent accommodation during the hours they are not employed.
I know how difficult it is to find accommodation. I have in mind at the moment a gentleman who for over a week has been looking for a single room in which he may sleep. In some places landladies exact conditions which are neither right nor just. For example, a case I have before me indicates that girls who were paying a high price for a room were told, "You may sleep there, but you must be out of this room all day."
It seems to me it is the duty of the government and of parliament-because after all parliament is the expression of the will of the people, or ought to be-to do their utmost to remedy this situation. I have taken this opportunity to bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance and the committee. I do not know whether he is aware of it or not, but I may say to the minister that quite often it is said, "Not only can we not get building supplies, but even if we could get them the Minister of Finance or the treasury board would not let us erect these buildings." Indeed the Minister of Finance and the treasury board sometimes have to bear the brunt of criticism of the lack of social services and social amenities in this dominion. The stumbling block, we are told is, that the Minister of Finance or the treasury board is not seized of the need for improvements, but that is no excuse for parliament, and it is, I think, a bad excuse for the government. I urge the minister and the government to give consideration to this problem which so nearly affects the lives of a large number of young people in this city, particularly those who may in after years be the wives of the men who will return from overseas and become the mothers of the future generations of Canadians.

I desire to say a word about this problem. The condition of the young girls who have arrived in Ottawa

to take war-time positions was called to my attention very soon after I had assumed the responsibility of this position. On that occasion the question was the rate of salary paid to these young girls, and I felt it incumbent upon me to urge upon the treasury board or the civil service commission or whoever was seized with authority a revision of their salaries. I am glad to be able to say that that has been done. As to whether or not it has been done adequately,-1 do not at the moment desire to express any opinion.
Recently there has been borne in upon me other aspects of their conditions, as presented by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I do not know whether the experience of other hon. members is the same as mine, but frequently some young girl whom perhaps I know personally from my own community calls upon me for assistance in this respect. I certainly know that my colleague the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) is called upon every week to go out and find a boarding place for some young girl who has come to the city to take war work, and he is often driven to his wit's end to accomplish that which he desires to do. I have had the same experience of being appealed to, but fortunately I have had the cooperation of a good staff, which has, to a large extent, relieved me of responsibility.
There is a distinct governmental responsibility in this matter. The government has centralized war services in Ottawa, and when it does that it must assume responsibility for the housing of these young girls, and not leave the responsibility to the community. The government may say: "That is all very well, but the city of Ottawa is reaping some benefit from having these government employees here." That just begs the question. We are inviting these young people to come to Ottawa to help carry on the national war effort, and we are centralizing all these war services in this city. But we do not do a thing to provide decent accommodation for these employees, especially for these young girls, many of whom are away from home for the first time. The same problem with respect to war workers moving from one state to another has arisen in the United States. I recall reading last winter an article in the Atlantic Monthly which put the case very fairly for the municipalities, saying that since the government had created the condition, the government must assume the responsibility, not only for the housing of these people but for sanitary services, for school services, and for their hospitalization if these services became beyond the capacity of the local community.

War Appropriation-Finance
We ask these people to come to Ottawa. They come, many of them not knowing what the situation is here. When they get here they find themselves at the mercy of a lot of people who make their living by this means- and I am casting no aspersions on the landlords or landladies of Ottawa because I do not know enough about the circumstances. But I do know that there is a responsibility on the government to deal with this problem.
I do not think the letter of the Prime Minister's secretary to the municipal officials is satisfactory. I think the government has to grapple with this problem, and the sooner it grapples with it, the better. I make this concrete suggestion. I ask the government to set up a representative committee of civil servants to meet with the council of the city of Ottawa with a view to coming to a conclusion as to what shall be done. Let there be cooperation on both sides.
I think the suggestion of a women's hostel is perhaps the most satisfactory suggestion that [DOT]can be made. Of this I am certain, that something must be done to relieve the shortage of accommodation. The government must deal with the situation, and my suggestion is that they appoint a committee to meet with the city council and grapple with the situation with a view to building a hostel. The government can build offices on Wellington street and furnish them at the rate of $500 a room, as we have heard has been done. I have heard of a man wanting to move in his own mahogany furniture, but that was stopped as likely to give rise to great scandal. Some man was furnishing his room with an $800 carpet, but in that case the government was not paying for the carpet but the man himself.
To allow these girls just to look after themselves is not good enough. Let us deal with the situation with humanity, even if we are at war. I do not want it to be thought that the socialist party has any monopoly in the consideration of the humanitarian aspects of this problem. Other people are thinking about it too. The government can put up two buildings at great expense on Cartier square to house the navy. I am not critical of that, but they are just temporary buildings to be torn down after the war. Is not the welfare of these young girls who are brought to Ottawa a matter of paramount importance to us all and to the future welfare of this nation? Then let the government set up a committee right away and get in touch with the city council with a view to building hostels and providing other necessary services too. They will be doing a good job for which they will be acclaimed, I believe, by the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will see that that suggestion is given most respectful and serious consideration. It is not primarily my responsibility; I am not the minister, to see to the housing of civil servants, but naturally I take an interest in the matter. Although I do not know too much about it I have some idea of what the situation has been, and I think the appointment of a committee or board or commission is a good idea. I believe that will have to be done. I think the composition of that board, its representative nature, will have to be given serious consideration, because the operation by the government of a girls' hostel will be a difficult and responsible task. I know that when the question was discussed last fall as to whether a hostel should not be built then to accommodate five or six hundred girls, the very suggestion almost was getting us into trouble because this interest and that interest were starting out to insist that they must have representation on any board that had charge of an enterpise of that kind. So far as the time to do this is concerned, we should pursue the same rule that we try to observe with our war effort generally; that is, that so long as persons coming here can find accommodation in the houses which are available at the present time, they should do so, even at some considerable inconvenience. If anyone thinks the people of this country in the next two or three years are going to escape inconvenience in housing, he is entirely wrong.
The construction programme of the government this year for military purposes, I am told is larger-I was going, to say twice as large, but I may be wrong in my proportions -than in any previous year. That may be surprising to members of this committee, but that is what I was told by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply the other day. There is going to be the most terrific scramble for materials for housing in all parts of Canada, and we must keep it down to the very minimum.
Well, the same crowd gave priority for a beer warehouse.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right, now. Every hon. member will be able to think of something for which he would not have given a permit if he had been director of construction. Certainly anyone is able to do that. The controller of construction is in the Department of Munitions and Supply. He has a very difficult task to perform, and, no doubt, is discharging it as best he can. He has certain rules applicable to residential construction, certain rules applicable to industrial construction, and so forth. He has kept construction down much better than private construction would have
War Appropriation-Finance

been restrained had there been no control. There must be rigid and severe control over construction, which will entail a considerable amount of inconvenience. Of course, that inconvenience cannot pass a certain stage. All I want hon. members to understand is that there is likely to be some, and that the government is keeping an eye on that situation and will give it serious consideration. My understanding-and here I may simply be provoking controversy, for I do not know very much about the matter-is that the situation in Ottawa eases in the spring and becomes a little harder in the fall, because in the spring people move out to various country cottages in the vicinity; and I do not think there will be an impossible situation or a very inconvenient situation during the summer and early fall months.
That possibility is going to be wiped out on account of the gasoline restrictions.
What about next fall?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that; the
obvious answer is that we should be thinking of the situation next fall, and I may say that we are thinking of it. The suggestion of a board or a commission is a very good one.

As regards these temporary buildings which are being erected in Ottawa: Canada is growing; the public service of Canada is growing; accommodation is needed to house government employees. Canada has now been at war for nearly three years, and there has been plenty of opportunity and time to build a few more permanent buildings. I believe the government would have been better advised to construct a few permanent buildings, instead of temporary buildings, at a great expense, which will have to be destroyed after the war. Take the Lord Elgin hotel: it was built inside a year. There is no reason why the government cannot erect permanent office buildings right here in the city. They will be available for all time to come, and the expense in the long run will be less than the cost of putting up these mushroom buildings and afterwards tearing them down.
And it would avoid the fire risk.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to certain remarks made earlier, I believe, by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) gave us the trade history of that delicious seafood known as the lobster. This 
statement interested me very much, although there remain a great many things to be said on the subject, for my constituency and more particularly the Magdalen islands produce a great deal of lobster, in fact, a large percentage of our entire Canadian output.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to remind the hon. member that we are now considering the auditor general's report. No one has objected to the hon. member's remarks, but it is incumbent upon me to direct the debate according to the rules of the house. I merely wish to draw the hon. member's attention to the item now under consideration, and to say that I do not believe there is a sufficiently close connection between it and the situation with regard to fisheries in Gaspe or the lower St. Lawrence, to warrant the latter's discussion.

Begging your pardon, Mr. Chairman, I was under the impression that the S3,000 item which I notice here had brought about, earlier in the day, a discussion on this subject, and the remarks I have to make are directly related to the state of war.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I am not mistaken, the hon. Minister of Fisheries' remarks were intended to correct an unfair criticism of the auditor general's report. It had been alleged that in his report, the auditor general might have been more explicit with regard to the expenditures incurred by the fisheries department. The minister then explained the scope of the auditor general's report with regard to fisheries. Any remarks made in this connection must be directly related to the report under consideration.
Can I not make certain observations at the moment, Mr. Chairman, provided they are directly concerned with the state of war?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, not unless they are related to the auditor general's report.
Very well.

May I briefly supplement the remarks I made last evening to offer some suggestions to the minister about what I think should be done with regard to auditing and checking these war accounts, the item of $196,000.
In the first place I want to point out to the minister that it is not an audit at all; it is just a checking system. Those of us who have come up from the municipalities have had some experience in this work. The system we have to-day of auditing and checking with relation to war expenditures

War Appropriation-*Finance
is just a village system; it is not and never was designed for such a great war as this, where in one year we are going to spend $2,200 millions. There are twenty-five of these various bodies which are called corporate instrumentalities. Many of these bodies are themselves spending bodies, and they have their own auditors. I contend that we should have a new consolidated revenue and audit act; there should be a committee of the house which would be known as the audit committee, and they might be a ways and means or finance committee. It would greatly help the minister, who is bearing a very heavy burden at this time. I regret to have to bring this matter up, but I believe the discussion will do a great deal of good and strengthen the government in the end. As one goes about the country he finds that everybody is aware of this or that condition of waste or duplication, and there is nobody to stop it. The auditor general is responsible to parliament. All he does is get out a great big book, the auditor general's annual report, which I doubt if anybody ever reads; I know I have not read it since 1926 or 1927, till last year. For the auditing and checking of war work, there should be a standard system of audit to apply to the government and all outside boards. No bank or insurance company could keep open its doors a month if it were to run on the kind of village system of checking accounts we have. No county council could discharge its duties and no public utility could carry on with such an antiquated system.
I suggest that we should adopt the practice which prevails in England. First, there should be a standard form of audit; second, there should be a committee of the house known as the ways and means and audit committee to which the minister could send the auditor general's report for revision.
I looked over some of the work here. I may say that I was told away back in 1926-27 that the audit system was all right, when I first had the matter up with the late Mr. Robb who was then Minister of Finance. Mr. Robb was an able minister who knew a great deal about business, and competitive business too. At that time I took exception to the audit system, but everyone said that the audit was all right. Of course, every audit is all right until there is an explosion and it is discovered that money has been squandered. There are a good many business men both in this house and in the other place who have impressive financial names, and they know that one of the greatest necessities to-day, at Washington, in London and in Canada, in connection with our various large institutions,
is the conservation of money and capital through a proper up-to-date system of checking and auditing and retrenchment, concentration, and the elimination of waste and duplication. But what have we here? There is no system at all, as far as I can see. In the first place, what is an audit? A modern, up-to-date audit must recommend changes; it must eliminate waste, and it must find out if there is coordination and cooperation among the various departments that go to make up the minister's budget. Here we have, according to page 541 of the auditor general's report, twenty-five of these outside boards under the department, and yet there is no control over most of them. Apart from two or three cases, what the government should do is to take over all these various outside boards, the whole twenty-five of them and audit the whole system. Toronto had to do that very thing with its outside boards. Toronto's financial affairs are much larger than the finances of the province of Ontario, with its outside boards, and the city had to adopt a new audit system and1 a new system for the sale of bonds and for capital levies. There had been no protection in the old days for the taxpayers from duplicate systems of handling loans, and the city decided to appoint Mr. Bradshaw to look after all the work, to make provision in connection with bonds, capital charges, and so on, dealing with thousands of employees and very large public utilities engaged in the handling of money running into a hundred million dollars and more. The result of that new system was a great economy, coupled with efficiency. There could be a great deal of saving to-day if the minister would adopt a new audit system, with a veto power.
When I first came into this house in 1926 and 1927, I was told that, for instance, the banks were solvent, that no bank had failed. But what happened? The Home bank closed its doors because the system of inspection was a myth. Some of the directors and others took millions of dollars out of the till, and invested the money in the United States, putting it into other pockets. Yet we were told at the time that the bank inspection and audit and checking system were all right. We were told that it could not happen here, but it did. When Mr. Robb was Minister of Finance I brought this whole question up in the house because I could foresee the explosion. I knew there was going to be trouble in connection with the insurance companies, and I brought in a bill in relation to audit and checking in reference to the large insurance companies, to provide that no insurance company should be allowed to invest trust
War Appropriation-Finance

funds, that is insurance funds, extra-territorially in common stocks. An investigation by the auditor general and others, disclosed in the insurance report submitted by the inspector of insurance, showed that hundreds of millions of trust funds were taken out of the country and invested in South Sea bubbles the world over, in what are known as common stocks of these companies, with the result that the money was lost. My bill to prevent these investments in such common stocks outside Canada went before the banking and commerce committee, but the proposed amendment was defeated and millions and millions were lost and squandered at that time. But they said that the system was perfect. Well, no system is perfect, and certainly we have not a proper system. It is all very well to check up a pay sheet with 181 names on it, but nobody knows how they got there.
I can tell the committee something about these outside federal government boards. In Toronto I see a good deal of waste about the streets in war expenditures, and anyone who travels over the country on our trains, visiting different places, will observe war waste all along the line. Of course there will be waste. There was waste in the days of Napoleon and in the days of Pitt, and it is only to be expected that there will be waste in the conduct of a war like this. But when the government is expending two billion dollars^vhen it is dealing with astronomical figuiro, it should put on the brakes and see that the money is well spent. In England the war expenditures committee has recommended changes, according to the report which has arrived to-day and which I have seen. It has recommended changes in auditing and checking of accounts, coordination, revision and veto power, with the result that in the old country they have saved hundreds of thousands of pounds by means of their up-to-date system. They have had a house-cleaning, and we should have the same. That is one thing that can be said to the credit of the late auditor-general, Mr. McDougall, whose name was an influence in the Victorian era here, and an influence with those that came after him. He vetoed hundreds of items.
But what do we find here? Here I can find only one item vetoed last year from the treasury board. I contend that the auditor-general, who has to report to parliament, should have power to veto any expenditure he sees fit. Look at the five or six departments in which there is so much duplication and waste at the present time. There is utter waste in these departments, for the simple reason that five different bodies have been spending money like water. They have been putting up duplicate billboards such as the one that says

"No loyal citizen hoards". They have put out billboards, advertisements, booklets, the height of the parliament building; there has been no equal to it since the tower of Babel in waste paper and talk. There would be no place in which to house the billboards and publicity material if we wanted to.
The tax-payers are getting sick and tired of this sort of thing. The government is all the time taking more money from the taxpayer than he can afford to pay. We are supposed to have a comptroller of the treasury, but all he does is to have a few clerks look up and check accounts. As for the checking system we have, I would not give five cents for it. I have seen some of these accounts, and I know there is duplication and waste. For example, there are two bodies in Toronto, one military and the other under the civil service commission, and for two years now there has been conflict between the civil body and the air force. The commission claim the power to appoint bookkeepers, stenographers, clerks, checkers and so on, and yet there is the Royal Air Force over their head with a duplicate staff spending more money, and making these appointments illegally.
Again, there is the Department of Munitions and Supply. I admire the minister, and I am fair enough to admit that he has done splendid work. There is, however, some waste in the department in the camp established. It cannot continue much longer. Take these outside boards; we have pages and pages of publicity material in the newspapers every day coming from these various boards. There is hardly a small retailer who can carry on with the interference of those bureaucrats, mostly untrained in business. One the other day said at a meeting that the small retailer may have to close up for lack of materials.
I submit that we shall have to change our way of doing business; otherwise this high court of parliament may as well be abolished for all the control we have over these war expenditures and over outside commissions and boards after the money is spent, and they are all postmortems. You have here, largely for civil government, an amount of $146,000,000, some overdraft, and there are draft estimates that came out a few days after parliament met, but the committee of supply has not yet sat one day. There has never been any committee of supply to pass upon one dollar of these estimates. We are supposed to have a break-down here. Well, it is a break-down because you cannot get any detailed information on each item from the minister. There are no details of expenditures, no details of these large items running into millions of dollars. I repeat, we shall have to change the whole system.

War Appropriation-Finance
I suggest that the Minister of Finance should have a fixed day for bringing down his budget; there should be a fixed day for the annual submission of his budget and for audits and accounting. How can you provide a proper audit and checking system when one person, the Minister of Finance, can say, "I will produce my budget, if I choose, in June." The accounts should be balanced up to the end of December and a proper audit made at that time and the financial year end with the calendar year. The date for the submission of the auditor general's report is fixed by statute, and there should be a similar provision applying to the Minister of Finance in the bringing down of his budget. Here we have two-thirds of the budget before us in connection with war expenditures nearly spent. It means that the budget speech is brought down afterwards as a sort of postmortem. Now are we going to have half a dozen budget speeches instead of coordinating them into one? The country is heading for national bankruptcy. These are strenuous days for the poor retailer and wholesaler; they are driven to the wall with artificial controls. I do not wish to embarrass the minister, far from it, but I believe that this discussion will strengthen his hands and do a great deal of good, and that it will be discussed in the country. It will not be possible to increase the income tax or obtain any further money unless we retrench and get value for our money-either income taxes or death duties or anything else, and the government may never collect any proposed increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The next item is "comptroller of the treasury."

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: After external affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will skip external affairs for the moment.
Are we including the item mentioned in the same line, "dependents' allowance office"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; the item is:
Comptroller of the treasury, dependents' allowance office and outside establishments, $4,979,617.

When the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) brought his estimates before the house I called attention to the condition of the dependents of our men in the forces as I had observed them in the riding from which I come. The Minister of National Defence for Air then informed us that he would discuss with his colleagues the question of granting a cost of living bonus to these dependents. I understand that this dependents' board was set up
on November 14 last. Four days before that board was set up a deputation came to the Minister of Finance from Toronto representing certain organizations interested in our men in the forces and overseas. It was the considered opinion of those representatives that the cost of living bonus was a much more satisfactory solution of this problem than that proposed by the minister at the time. I am further informed that the minister asked that deputation to give his plan a fair trial. I have here correspondence from the ladies auxiliary of the Royal Canadian Engineers, and am assured by that organization that after having given the minister's plan a trial they are convinced that this board and the granting of dependents' allowances to the wives and families of men in the forces do not constitute a solution of the problem.
In the first place it has the appearance of charity. These wives must admit to their homes social service workers, who are required to check the family budget to discover whether they can advise the soldier's wife where and-how she can make her budget go further. Then application is made through the social service representative; if approved, it is sent on to Ottawa, and, if it is approved by Ottawa, the dependents in the course of two or three months receive a cheque. While this board was set up in November, I understand that the first payments did not reach the families in Toronto until the winter months had passed; it was along some time in March or April before many of the dependents were receiving any allowances from this board.
I understand that the stock argument in favour of this board and against the cost of living bonus is that some of these wives are unable to manage their own affairs, unable to manage their budget economically. That may be true of a small percentage of them. Social service workers have estimated that it is true of probably two per cent of the dependents. The fact remains that these families managed their own affairs while their husbands were in Canada. They are asking to-day why it is that they should be the one class of citizens to be discriminated against in this respect. Practically every other group of citizens below certain wage levels are granted the cost of living bonus. In the great majority of these cases if the men had remained at home and gone to work in war or other industries the families would be receiving cost of living bonus to-day. They and their families are being penalized because they showed sufficient patriotism to enlist in the forces. I maintain that one of the great deterrents to enlistment to-day is the sight across the road of a
War Appropriation-Finance

soldier's wife and family who have to depend upon what to all intents and purposes is charity to secure sufficient money to get by.
I should like to read to the committee one or two short extracts from letters from the officials of the ladies auxiliary to the Royal Canadian Engineers on this question. It is pointed out here that social service workers came into twelve typical homes in Toronto and tried to find ways and means whereby these wives could do better than they were doing with the income at their disposal. Matters came to such a strait that a number of these wives offered to turn over their homes, their children, the management of their homes to social service workers in order that the wives themselves might work out and earn something for their own subsistence. There is a standing offer made to these social service workers to come in and manage a dozen of these homes to see if it can be done any better than it is being done by the women in charge. So far no offer of that kind has bee.n accepted.
I have one paragraph here which expresses the feeling of those people. They say:
Just because possibly 2 per cent of dependents are indiscreet, poor managers, unable to handle funds to the best advantage, does that mean that we must all be "assisted" by social service workers or starve and freeze; failing that we can "make application" humbly I suppose for "assistance"-they don't like it called "charity", and if the committee gives favourable consideration the "award is recommended." Do the powers that be feel that all dependents are unable to manage their own affairs? Do they feel that all dependents should be shoved and bandied about in this way? Is their contribution to the war effort not great enough without being subjected to this indignity?
I am sure this matter has been taken up with the minister on a number of occasions, but I should like to direct his attention also to one case history which has been brought to my notice. It is pointed out here that in many of these families there is a sickness allowance. The regional committee in Toronto has on record cases of sickness, particularly of children, caused through nothing but insufficient food of the proper kind, or in fact food of any kind; lack of warmth in the home because of insufficient coal, and so on. One woman with four children had seven cases of measles in the home last summer and two cases of tonsilitis. During the winter the children were continually ill with colds. At the present time three children in that family are so underweight that the authorities have put them in the open-air school, while the fourth is being given extra milk at school in order to provide the child with sufficient strength to carry on the school work. I made the statement formerly that there were families 
in my riding worse off to-day than they were when the father was at home on relief. Since making that statement I have received letters from social workers in that riding assuring me that this is an actual fact. I have here a statement signed by certain teachers in a school in a district adjoining Toronto. They say:
It has been brought to our attention through charity organizations that there are instances in York township where a soldier's pay is inadequate to keep the family. It has been stated there are cases where the family received more on relief than it now receives in the armed forces.
We, the undersigned, as citizens in your riding, feel that the wives of the armed forces and the children, regardless of their number, should receive adequate financial compensation to relieve them from accepting charity. It is the least that can be done for families of men standing between the enemy and ourselves.
That is signed by thirty teachers in one of the schools attended by some of these children. I think it is generally agreed that the dependents' allowance serves a good purpose, in cases of sickness, where hospitalization is needed, and in the case of families with more than four children, since the government grants allowance for only four. But the point about which these dependents are concerned, the question they are asking, is why the family of the industrial worker should get a cost of living bonus while the family of the soldier cannot get it. I have been told by social workers in that district that they have great difficulty in restraining these women from mass demonstrations of their indignation against the government for its refusal to grant them this cost of living bonus. So I would seriously ask the Minister of Finance to consider the possibility of giving the soldier's dependents a cost of living bonus similar to that being given others in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I believe this matter was taken up on the defence estimates; at least I am so informed. At any rate that is the place where it should be taken up. The only reason why the dependents' allowance office appears in here is because part of the vote of 84,979,617 is for the expenses of the officers of the comptroller of the treasury who pay the accounts that are payable through that office.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); Administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. Any matter of policy, so far as the amount that should be paid is concerned, is for another department, not for the Department of Finance. Probably the hon. gentleman has in mind that last November, when dealing with a large number of demands on the government for cost of living

War Appropriation-Finance
bonuses, it fell to my lot to deal with those demands because a statement could not be made by each of a number of ministers. It was essentially one matter, and I dealt with all the demands. Last fall we were confronted with demands for cost of living bonuses from old age pensioners, from those receiving war veterans' allowances, from superannuated civil servants and others whom I do not seem to remember. Some hon. member says "mothers' allowances." I do not think they applied to this government, because mothers' allowances are paid by the provincial governments. At any rate, at that time we had to decide what policy we were going to follow in reference to the payment of cost of living allowances; whether everyone in the country whose position w7as worsened by the increased cost of living was to receive a cost of living allowance, or whether we were to stick to the original intention of our cost of living allowance policy, which was part of our wage policy and nothing else. We decided we would do that. In regard to these dependents' allowances, I do not understand that the hon. gentleman wishes to drop our present system and turn to the cost of living allowance system.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member wants both systems; he says that this system is of value in case of sickness, where there are more than four children in the family, and so on. We do not think both systems are necessary.
With regard to dependents' allowances, it must be remembered that the experience we had to go on was the experience of the last war, when wives received a separation allowance of $25, during a period such as this, and at the end received a separation allowance of $30, at a time when the cost of living was far higher than it is at the present time. That is, it was only at the end of the war that it went up to $30. There was no allowance at all for the children. They were provided for out of what was called the Patriotic fund, which fund was administered by public-spirited citizens who voluntarily contributed money. At the beginning of this war what was normally to be expected was an increase in the cost of living, so at the outset we made the wife's allowance $35, which was $5 more than it was at the end of the last war, when the cost of living was much higher. We also provided allowances for children as of right, and in November we increased those allowances to cover up to four instead of only two children. There is a group-I will not say it is entirely confined to Toronto, but it centres in that city-which has written a great many letters,
has come to see us several times, and has conducted a very earnest agitation-and I do not say that in any invidious sense-for the extension of the cost of living bonus to these dependents' allowances on principle, and that has been joined in by several members of this house. I was in the house one day when the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) was making a very earnest plea to the government to add to this cost of living bonus; that is, since it was $35 at the beginning of the war, and the'cost of living had gone up 15 per cent, it should be $40 now. Apparently his argument was that, once having set the amount at $35, the government was-I will not say "hooked"-but committed to that amount, and that it should increase according to the increased cost of living.
I am not the one to whom the agitation was directed, although I received the delegation on one or two occasions. In addition, I have received many letters from the delegation in language very much like the language the hon. member has just used. But I am sure that in many parts of the country the system we have adopted is regarded as, if not completely, at least reasonably satisfactory. This perpetual harping on what they call charity-and the hon. member has identified himself with that group-is entirely unwarranted and entirely unjustifiable. There is no charity about the matter at all.
The government has come into this, very much the same as the Patriotic fund came in. But after making much wider and more binding provisions as of right for the wives and children, the government has put up a fund, where money is needed. In some localities the cost of living is much higher than in others. Rents may be higher in one place than another.
However, I have talked to people around the country who think the present provision is reasonably satisfactory. Of course that will not satisfy those hon. members who think money does not make any difference at all, and that we can pay unlimited amounts. But I do suggest that the government ought not to be accused of being indifferent, careless or unintelligent in the way it has handled this problem.

I was
rather startled to hear the hon. member make the assertion that the amount paid to the wife and children of a man on service was less than would have been received had he been on relief. I can scarcely credit that. From memory I have put down some figures respecting the amount paid to a soldier with a wife and four children, and if my premises are correct that amounts to $113 a month, made
War Appropriation-Finance

up as follows: pay, $39; allowances, $35; $12 for the first child, $12 for the second, $9 for the third and $6 for the fourth. Twelve times that amount would be $1,356. I wonder if any municipality in this country ever paid that much in relief. If it did not, then that just shows an exaggeration which is not justified by the facts.
Further than that, my understanding of the policy of the government was that it would make the allowance from the very beginning, thereby doing away with a patriotic fund such as we had in the last war, under which some people gave a great deal and others gave very little. I understood the purpose was to spread it among the taxpayers of -the country, where it belonged as a matter of business and not as a matter of charity.
Is there anything to the suggestion that the family to which reference has been made received more by way of relief than under present circumstances?

That statement was made to me by reliable social service workers, and I believe it applied to the case of very large families. In York South men, with eight or ten children at home, have joined the army. I can well believe they would be worse off under the allowance they are getting now-or were getting a few months ago, because I do not know what arrangements have been made since-than they were when they were on relief.
Did the hon. member check up, or is this hearsay?

As to charity, may I point out that these women object strenuously to having social service workers come into their homes, checking their budgets and checking their outlay in connection with home management, and then making applications for allowances. To them this looks like charity- whether it is or not. That is one objectionable feature.

This is an item of about $21,000 less than $5,000,000, to the comptroller of the treasury for dependents' allowance, and it is made available to the dependents' allowance board. I am reminded of the provision made last fall with respect to men having more than two children. The minister surprises me very much, because all the time he seems to be offering special pleading against benefits for soldiers. For instance, there was the high cost of living bonus I supported, with an allowance for those with more than two children; then there was the matter of soldiers' insurance, free fares, and other matters of that kind.
This department is spending vast sums of money, but I have never seen anything in my

life like the way it is using returned soldiers, their wives and children. I believe if the minister had attached to his department a few soldiers who had served in the great war, it would be a much better department, and they would give the soldier and his dependents a break.
The public is not objecting to these war expenditures, if they are made in an all-out war effort and the soldiers given better treatment. But when we look at this list of payments we immediately see one for $50,000,000 to pay for subsidies under the priceceiling order. While this large sum is made available for that purpose, there is not a cent for the soldier who is fighting our battles and his dependents. History will deal with those who have been responsible for that kind of work. I ask the minister to come down out of the clouds, and let something be done for our soldiers who are fighting our battles. I am sick and tired of hearing special pleading by the government when any matter of this kind comes up. Despite all the boards there are around the country, the soldier is getting little or nothing. Not many of them are even remembered in connection with the amendment the minister made of a small insignificant grant, just charity, instead of a real cost of living bonus.
The provision made for those with more than two children was just a sop; it did not amount to a snap of the fingers. Very few benefited by going before a board. All over the country the government is setting up these new boards, but very few of the soldiers, if any, get one red cent out of it.
I am not going to vote for any more of these things until we have a fair and square deal for the soldier who is fighting our battles and his dependents. He is not getting it at the present time.

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I have in my hand
Beauchesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Second Edition", and I find that citation 502 reads:
The estimates for the year are submitted to the committee of supply by the finance minister bringing them down in the house with a message from the governor general which is read in English and French, the house standing, by the Speaker or by the clerk at the table. The minister then moves "that the said message, together with the estimates, be referred to the committee of supply." The estimates are after-v-ards taken up at any time the government thinks proper.

War Appropriation-Finance
According to the explanation that was given by the minister this afternoon, these estimates are part of the $2,000,000,000 appropriation for war purposes, and so I ask, why is the procedure different in this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because this money is not to be voted item by item. This appropriation is part of a bill, and this is the procedure that is followed by parliament in all appropriations of money by bills. If, for instance, we were to pass a bill, as we are doing, to set up a scheme of war risk insurance, and the bill provides that $5,000,000 shall be appropriated and placed in the hands of an insurance organization to be set up by the government for the purpose, the consideration of that appropriation of $5,000,000 goes, not to the committee of supply but to the committee of the whole house. That is the uniform rule applied to appropriations provided by statute. When we have estimates, whioh are submitted to the House of Commons by His Excellency the Governor General, the committee of supply procedure applies, the procedure which the hon. gentleman has just mentioned, and the committee of supply deals with those estimates item by item. But we do not go to the committee of supply with a bill of this kind.

I am sorry I cannot agree with the minister. There is, of course, a difference between estimates and grants; they are not the same thing at all. The kind of expenditure we are now discussing is called an appropriation, but simply because it is called an appropriation I do not believe that the procedure should be changed. The procedure should be the same as when the appropriations are just the ordinary estimates. A grant is something special, something out of the ordinary. But when we come to consider the expenditures of a department, even if there is some increase, they still remain estimates, and so I submit that the procedure should be the same and that this appropriation should come before the house in the usual way that estimates come. I know very well that if Mr. Bennett or Mr. Meighen or Mr. King or Sir Wilfrid Laurier or Sir Robert Borden had been the leader of the opposition at this time, he would have protested strongly against this procedure.
I am to blame, I suppose.

My hon. friend the leader of the opposition may strike his bosom; nevertheless he has a responsibility in this
matter-
Mea culpa.
I cannot understand this procedure at all. This appropriation should have been brought before the committee of supply in the usual way, with a message from the governor general.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman raise a point of order?

I am just submitting a
question, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The resolution was
introduced into the house by the minister, and the minister stated that it had' received the approval of the governor general and that it was recommended by his excellency to the house. That is the usual procedure with money bills. The resolution has been referred by the house to the committee of the whole. The point raised by the hon. member might have been raised and discussed in the house at the time when the motion was made to refer the resolution. I do not believe it is within the jurisdiction of the committee now to discuss the question on a point of order.

If you will permit me,
Mr. Chairman, in the first place the whole matter was put on record by the Minister of Finance when nobody knew what was involved. Of course, the minister made a few preliminary remarks, and it was just because the members were not at all familiar with what had been put on Hansard that discussion was postponed. What the minister put on record was not submitted by way of a special motion.
It was just put on record when the Chairman was in the Chair, not yourself, Mr. Chairman, but an acting chairman, and I had just started to ask a question of the Minister of National War Services when I was told that we were going to proceed with finance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The resolution
was placed on the order paper. When it had been on the order paper for the prescribed period, it was taken up by the house, with His Honour the Speaker in the Chair. A motion was made that this resolution be read a first time, and, then, that it be referred to the committee of the whole. If some hon. members did not notice it, the matter can no longer be discussed here. This committee has been properly seized, without protest, of this resolution, and the action taken by the house is not subject to review by this committee at this stage.
War Appropriation-Finance

I do not know, Mr. Chairman, whether I am in order after your ruling in raising a question respecting the administration of the dependents' allowance legislation which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. Am I in order in doing that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say a word on that? If the hon. gentleman is proposing to discuss a decision of the dependents' allowance board, that should have been discussed under national defence. If he has in mind some administrative action of the comptroller of the treasury, who is merely in this case a cheque-signing and sending officer, it is in order under this. But I think it is important to keep that distinction in mind, because this is an item to pay the expenses of the comptroller of the treasury for sending out money for various war departments, and this is one of them. I would ask hon. members, having fully discussed the subject of dependents' allowances when national defence was before the committee, to refrain from discussing it under this finance item.

As a matter of expediency and convenience, what the minister is suggesting is correct, but under an administrative item I think a member of the House of Commons has the right to discuss any matter that requires redress of grievances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would just point out that if the position taken by the leader of the opposition is correct, there is no limit whatever to any part of our war expenditure that can be discussed now, because the comptroller of the treasury pays all the bills-
I expect that is true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and under this item the whole field can be ranged over. For the sake of expediency, if for no other reason, I do not think we should go over these matters time after time. There would be no need to call in any other minister if this could be done.

The matter I wish to discuss is directly connected with the administration as it applies to outlying districts in our province. At the present time apparently the dependents' allowance board have no way of deciding-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Does the hon. gentleman address his remarks to a special item relative to the war, or is he discussing the general administration of the dependents' allowance legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I was going to say something about this dependents' allowance, but I do not see any reason for kicking a dead horse. The point is, I was here last year in connection with this matter; a delegation came from Toronto, and we had a nice hearing, but we did not get any place on the question of a bonus to dependents. The salaries which have been paid to clerical help, mostly women, may be considered in this way: take a girl earning $70 a month; she is allowed a cost of living bonus; but we cannot go any higher; we may not give her more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On a point of order, can we not keep to some rule of discussion here? Otherwise, I again say, there will be no end to this discussion. having regard to the fact that the defence estimates are through. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I shall quote May on "Parliamentary Practice," at page 521:
The committee of supply controls the public expenditure by considering the grants of money that will be required for the army, navy, air force, and civil services (including revenue departments) during the current year.

If I am correct in that premise, then I submit with great respect that the Chair is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Surely the question of dependents' allowance was discussed by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston).
I am discussing the technical aspect of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In the first place, we are not in committee of supply, and in the second place we are concerned only with an item of $4,979,000. May I submit, on a point of order-
