speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will give the items making up the $4,979,617 and perhaps the hon. gentleman can bring his remarks under one of these. If he can, I have no objection, but I would ask members to confine their remarks to the items as we take them up; otherwise we shall ramble all over the whole field. This amount is made up as follows: Salaries, temporary, $3,901,752; cost of living bonus, $217,865; travelling expenses and subsistence allowance, $200,000; printing and stationery, $350,000; rental of equipment, $135,000; sundries, $175,000. This makes a total of $4,979,617. It will be remembered that the salaries to which I have referred are salaries of employees and officials of the comptroller of the treasuiy.

Salaries are what I wish to discuss, and I want to compare the situation. I can do it within the department itself or within any one of many departments. In the earlier days of the war we had people coming to Ottawa and offering their services, and they got into one position so that the only increases in salaries they can get now are increases which are due to promotion. In the city of Ottawa to-day a young woman getting only $70 a month and having to pay her board is having a pretty tough time, and the next thing she knows, a new and inexperienced girl is taken on. She is taken on because they cannot get them at less than $90 or $100 or $120. We know this is so. Moreover, they have not the experience of the girls who have been in for some time, but because of the wage ceiling these older girls cannot get anything but the cost of living bonus. The same situation exists in private enterprise. We must preserve certain of these essential industries, and we find all over the place that girls are leaving because the company itself cannot raise salaries to the level being paid for girls in the service. There exist therefore these two classes: girls who have been in the service for some time who cannot get an increase, and girls in private industry who also are unable to get any increase. All I have to say is this.

There never was anything in the world that called so much for compulsory national selective service as this very situation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is discussing the classification of civil servants and the salaries attached to various employments under the Civil Service Act. I must rule such discussion out of order as not covered by this item.

What the hon. member is complaining of, if I apprehend it rightly, is that the government is competing against private industry and paying wages which private industry cannot pay, and that of course is true all over the country. The government is draining away from private industry some of their best employees because it is competing for them. The government is going into the professions and taking lawyers and so on. That is what the hon. member is arguing against. Certainly that is relevant.

What are the duties of officials of the treasury board? Can they override decisions and judgments handed down by the dependents' allowance board? When one applies for dependents' allowance investigators are sent out, and a complete investigation is made of every individual case, both in regard to the papers sent in and on the ground by an investigator. A decision is made, and the treasury board officials have in some instances, I believe, overridden the decision of the board. We did not always have treasury board officials. All auditing used to be done by the auditor general's department, but from 1933 on we have had these officials, and there are many of them. I do not know whether they are double-checking, but I should like the minister to give an explanation. Can these officials or can that board override decisions of the dependents' allowance board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me make this clear:
many hon. members, I am sure, confuse the treasury board and its organization with the comptroller of the treasury. We are discussing now the comptroller of the treasury and his officials.
Waiving the point of order with the consent of the committee, may I say that there is a section of the dependents' allowance regulations, No. 119, which allows certain discretionary grants to be made with the approval of the treasury board, and the treasury board sometimes refuses that approval.

Will the minister explain
the item, "premium for the purchase of Dominion of Canada registered stock"?

War Appropriation-Finance

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Canadian government
agreed to the redemption of certain securities held abroad. We refer to it often as repatriation of securities held in the United Kingdom. The procedure is as follows: The United Kingdom government obtained these securities, paying the market price for them. Some of those securities-I am talking about Dominion of Canada bonds-were at a premium; the United Kingdom government had to pay more than par for them. We paid to the United Kingdom government what it paid for them. There is no authority under any of our war loan acts or appropriation acts to pay a premium in that way, so we had to use the War Appropriation Act. And the premium up to a certain date was $725,000.
In other words, -this transaction would not be on a purely business basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; we paid the market
price that the United Kingdom had paid to the holders.
The government is carrying out an obligation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

On the item "wartime prices and trade board", on Monday and Tuesday when the estimates of the Minister of Finance were before the committee certain hon. members made reference to the so-called price-ceiling regulations. The Minister of Finance is responsible to the house for the administration of those regulations. I have been wondering if hon. members realize what a great responsibility is on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance at this time. It has been necessary for him to arrange the financial structure of this dominion so that the war can be carried on successfully so far as money is required for that purpose. Canada has had many great ministers of finance, but I do not think there has been any minister who has had a clearer understanding of our financial structure, or who has been better informed on finance generally, or who has been more industrious and capable, than the present Minister of Finance.
Order.

I am satisfied that all hon. members will agree with me when I say that in the long line of great ministers of finance Canada has had the present minister stands with the greatest of those great ministers.
I suppose this is all in order under the Chairman's ruling?
What item is this on?

This
eulogy of the Minister of Finance I am sure must be obnoxious to him, and I think it is contrary to the ruling you, sir, have just given.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No; I do not see that there is any conflict between the ruling given and what the hon. member is now saying. We are on the wartime prices and trade board administration, and any hon. member has the right either to eulogize or criticize that administration.
I was ruled out of order because I criticized the administration.
No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In the first place the hon. gentleman cannot at this time discuss a former ruling. Further, the hon. gentleman was called to order because he was discussing something which was not before the committee. We are now discussing the administration of the wartime prices and trade board. The hon. gentleman who has the floor is saying that he finds it very much to his liking.
Is there a subsidy on molasses?

I would point out that in former wars the enormous sums of money involved in this war were not then involved. Where previous ministers of finance dealt with thousands of dollars, our present minister is dealing with hundreds of thousands; where they dealt with hundreds of thousands, he is dealing with millions; and where they dealt with millions, he is dealing with billions. I would remind hon. members that it was his department that arranged the gift of a billion dollars to Great Britain.
Is that included in this item?
Not only did he arrange that gift to Great Britain, but he also arranged a loan of $700,000,000 to that country.
Has that anything to do with this item?

Nothing whatever. According to the Chairman's ruling it is entirely unwarranted.
War Appropriation-Finance
If hon. members will bear with me, I shall soon come to the item under discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is a point of order. It is that the gift of a billion dollars to Great Britain is not related to the item before the committee. I must rule that it is not; and further, that item of a billion dollars to Britain was the subject of a previous debate during the present session.
It is only the debate that cannot be referred to, not the item. Let us have a little consistency.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: For the purpose of the point of order, there is no difference between the debate and the item. The debate arises out of the item.

I shall not refer further either to the item or the debate. I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I always do. As far as my memory serves me, I have always found your rulings to be correct.
I am further satisfied that all hon. members agree with me when I say that our present Minister of Finance has had a very heavy burden to bear, that he has borne it well, and that he has given Canada great service during the time he has been Minister of Finance.
Among the various boards administered by this department is the wartime prices and trade board. In another place I said there were three great problems facing Canada at this time. There was the problem of supplying armaments of all kinds to our armed forces. There was the problem of securing men to produce those armaments and also to maintain, reinforce and increase our armed forces. There was also the problem of preventing a devastating period of inflation in this country. I will deal only with the last-mentioned problem to-night. To me, inflation is a cancerous growth gnawing at the body politic which, if not checked, will develop into a galloping disease that will leave only misery and disaster in its train. Inflation affects injuriously all classes of our citizens. First, it affects the poor. It affects the workingman and the farmer, bringing misery to all. For that reason this government should do all in its power to prevent a devastating period of inflation from taking place either at the present time or when this war is concluded. I believe all members of this house are opposed to inflation, though a number of hon. members have opposed the method chosen to control our money and credit. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), who is one of the outstanding economists of this continent, has opposed the 
method which was adopted by the government in bringing in that legislation. Speaking in this house in a previous debate-
What date?

Perhaps I am not absolutely in order; it was in a debate which was in progress on February 9 of this year. I need not quote his words, but he referred to inflation as illusive. During the present debate the leader of the opposition said, as reported at page 2925 of Hansard:
I am in favour of control in war time to prevent inflation, if it can be done by any kind of decent method.
It was the method to which the hon. gentleman objected, not the control of inflation itself. Then on Monday of this week the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said, as appears at page 2926 of Hansard:
I am not complaining that the government did attempt to control prices. I think it was the proper thing to do under the existing circumstances.
So, Mr. Chairman, practically all hon. members are in accord with the policy of the government in its attempt to control prices. What has the government attempted to do? It has endeavoured to keep prices within reasonable bounds. In his speech on September 20, 1941, the Prime Minister said:
By its policy the government hopes to avoid the fears, the sense of insecurity, the suffering and the profiteering which the inflation of price inevitably brings in its train. The measures now announced should help in winning the war, facilitate recovery and reconstruction.
I ask, was the government properly alarmed with respect to the rise in prices? Already there has been placed upon Hansard a record of the cost of living index. I propose to place it upon Hansard again, in order to impress upon hon. members the serious situation toward which this country was drifting in October last. The base figure is 100, being the average from 1935 to 1939, and the rise is shown as follows:
August, 1939	 100-8
November, 1939	 103-8
February, 1940	 103-8
August, 1940	 105-9
February, 1941	 108-2
March, 1941	 108-2
April, 1941	 108-6
May, 1941	 109-4
June, 1941	 110-5
July, 1941	 111-9
August, 1941	 113-7
September, 1941	 114-7
October, 1941	 115-5
Hon. members will see that there was a rise of almost six points in the first year of the war and that within a little over two years the

War Appropriation-Finance
cost of living index had risen by more than fifteen points. At that time the government, in a masterly stroke, passed regulations which it hoped would stabilize prices, wages and salaries. Never before had such drastic legislation been attempted in this or any other democratic country. In making the announcement the Prime Minister stated:
The action I am about to explain represents an experiment hitherto untried on this continent, and perhaps, having regard to its breadth and variety, hitherto untried ... by any free country anywhere.
Then Mr. James S. Duncan, who for some time was deputy minister of national defence for air, which position he held when the commonwealth air training plan was established in Canada; a man who gave freely of his ability in the establishment of that plan in Canada, speaking before a meeting in the city of Toronto, is reported as follows:
Mr. Duncan congratulated Mr. Ilsley "for the courage and vision you have shown" in introducing price and wage ceilings legislation -"the boldest economic measures which have ever been taken under similar circumstances in any country throughout the world."
If Canada has stopped an undue rise in prices; if Canada has prevented inflation, the credit for that belongs to those who have been responsible for bringing in and administering this legislation. I should refer to Mr. Donald Gordon, who is head of the wartime prices and trade board which, as we know, administers the regulations. Some hon. members may consider that he has too much power. Nevertheless I think we must all agree that he has had a difficult task, and that he has done it very well indeed. Also credit for what success has been attained is to a large extent due to the people of Canada who have been willing to accept the drastic regulations which have been imposed upon them.
I would refer particularly to the women of this country. They have accepted the regulations and have endeavoured to prevent a rise in prices. As hon. members have heard before, the women do 80 per cent of the retail purchasing in this dominion. The regulations could not be a success unless they had the support and endorsation of the people.
In making his announcement the Prime Minister further stated:
In a democratic country price control cannot succeed without the active support and cooperation of the masses of the people. It will require the cooperation and the support of all. Its success will depend not alone upon the government but equally upon the willingness of all who are affected to accept, and to accept cheerfully, the limitations imposed upon them as a necessary contribution to Canada's war effort.
I asked a moment ago if these regulations had succeeded. My answer to that question is that they definitely have succeeded, and that the imposition of these regulations has prevented inflation and has maintained price stability. It was never intended that these regulations should be a panacea or a cure-all for all the evils of rapidly rising prices. The Prime Minister himself stated it was not hoped that they would be such a panacea.
According to the cost of living index, six months prior to the bringing in of the regulations the cost of living had risen approximately seven points. Six months have now passed since the regulations were brought in, and I am happy to say that the cost of living index has not risen even one point. That is indeed a great credit to those who conceived and to those who are carrying out the regulations.
We have heard a great deal about what is being done in the United States. I, along with all other hon. members in the committee, am indeed happy to know that the United States is doing such great things toward successfully prosecuting the war. However, in the house from time to time we have heard of the lack of what should be done by this country, and in many instances we have heard nothing but fault-finding with what has been done here. Indeed at times I feel that we are developing an inferiority complex with respect to our great war effort.
I am not going to quote further at this time from what people in Canada think about our price-fixing regulations. I would, however, draw the attention of the committee to a leading article which appears in this week's issue of the Saturday Evening Post, a magazine published in the United States. By the way, while this magazine sells for ten cents in the United States, due to price regulations in Canada it sells for only seven cents here.
The article is headed "Canada Did It." That is something new to hear in this committee. It is written by Congressman Albert Gore, and with the indulgence of the committee I should like to read these extracts from the article which I believe hon. members will find most refreshing. The opening paragraph is in these words:
One crisp Sunday morning last October, quite early, three men in a flurry boarded a Washington plane for Ottawa, Canada. The night before, Prime Minister Mackenzie King had announced the Canadian government's adoption of an over-all ceiling over prices, wages, salaries, services and rents-practically everything. And this was positively disturbing to the three agitated gentlemen and their chief, U.S. price boss Leon Henderson, for it came at a time when Mr. Henderson was marshalling arguments and strength to prevent a congressional committee from adopting a similar over-all-price-control bill.

War Appropriation-Finance

Then the article goes on to state that a certain time intervened, following which representatives of the United States came to Canada. The article continues:
In recent weeks, aides of price administrator Henderson had been shuttling back and forth between Washington and Ottawa. This time, it has not been to find reasons why the over-all plan should not be adopted, but to decide how much of Canada's plan the United States can copy.
The reason for this shift in attitude can be told in a few figures. In Canada, the cost of living index has remained constant since last November. In the United States, living costs have continued their relentless rise. The official Canadian cost-of-living index actually shows a slight decrease from a high of 115-4 in November to 115 in February. In the United States, despite all piecemeal-selective-[DOT] controls, it rose 2-4 points from November to February.
Canada stopped prices from rising. Her composite index of wholesale prices remained virtually fixed from November to February, rising only eight-tenths of one point in this time. During the same period wholesale prices in the United States rose 4-3 points. But more significant than index figures, the United States plan had failed.
What is that published in?
In the Saturday Evening Post of June 6, 1942, and it is written by Congressman Albert Gore.
Is that not an anti-British, isolationist paper?

I would say that this article is anything but anti-Canadian. It is a boost for Canada, and I think we should all be happy to hear a boost for Canada, from the United States, read in this chamber.
Mr. MacIN'NIS: Even though the Saturday Evening Post wrote it?

The article continues:
In adopting over-all controls, Canadians fully realized they were attempting a difficult undertaking. Prime Minister Mackenzie King called it an "experiment hitherto untried on this continent and perhaps .	. . hitherto untried
by the will and consent of free people anywhere."
Then the article refers to the reluctance and misgivings we had with respect to bringing these regulations into effect. The article then goes on to say:
The official Canadian cost-of-living index had risen 7 points in the 21 months from August, 1939, to April, 1941. It jumped approximately 8 points higher in the 7 months from April to November. Price rises were coming thick and fast. Wholesale prices rose approximately 12 per cent in the 7 months from March to October, 1941.

I would ask hon. members to mark these words:
Bold and effective action was necessary if Canada was to be saved from a wild runaway inflation. It was a hard choice, but Canada chose action-daring, adequate action.
That is what the United States thinks of the action which this country took to avoid inflation.

That is
the opinion of only one man. That is not the United States.

It
is the opinion of a congressman in the United States, which appears in a magazine read widely throughout the whole United States.
And which has been extremely antagonistic to this country.
The article goes on-

Put it on
Hansard.

I
am taking the liberty of reading part of the article to hon. members because I feel it should be good for the morale of the members of the committee to know what other countries are thinking about Canada. I will read one more sentence:
Now, despite its well-nigh incredible success to date, the programme has some hard tests in the months immediately ahead.
Yes; this legislation has hard tests in the months immediately ahead. During the last few days members from every part of this house have asked for increased prices. So far as I am concerned my sympathy is with those who are asking for increased prices. I would like to see all the farmers of this country get increased prices for their products where the price is not now adequate, and I would like to see all men who are working and receiving inadequate pay receive adequate pay. I am satisfied, I can say with confidence, that our government and our Minister of Finance are just as anxious as anyone else in this house that fair prices, fair wages and fair salaries should be given to all. But I would remind hon. members that if prices are increased and salaries and wages are increased, it serves little if the prices of the commodities they have to buy are also proportionately increased. There would be little gain for them in that. We cannot afford to have inflation in this country, even as we had it in the last war. It would not benefit the working man or the farmer to have increased wages and increased prices, if he at the same time had to pay

War Appropriation-Finance
such prices as 25 cents a pound for sugar as he had to do in the last war. It must be the object of our government and of parliament- and I think we should help the government in doing so-to keep prices down.
Every time there is an increase in prices it is a string on the present effort of the government to prevent inflation and to keep prices on a reasonable basis. We cannot stand too great a strain. If the Minister of Finance granted increases on all the products which have been mentioned in this house in the last few days, I am satisfied that our whole price structure would break down and we would start on that terrible course of inflation which in the end would bring only misery to all. My plea, Mr. Chairman, to members of this house is to support the Minister of Finance in his great effort to prevent inflation, to stabilize prices, wages and salaries. Let us try to make adjustments as soon as possible where adjustments must be made. Let us do what we can to provide labour for the farm at reasonable prices. But let us keep in mind that we must maintain our ceiling; we must not let it get out of bounds, and if we will give the Minister of Finance the support he deserves in this great undertaking, I am satisfied that when peace dawns it will bring prosperity and happiness to all.

We have just listened to a paean of praise from the hon. member for Brantford City for the policy of the government and to some fulsome flattery for the person of the Minister of Finance himself which I am sure he, with all his modesty, would have wished the member had not given utterance to, and incidentally thereby saved the time of the house.
At the risk of detaining the committee I wish to deal with this policy, which is a very important matter to the taxpayers of this country who are to be invited to pay to certain importers and producers next year in the way of subsidies in connection with the administration of this policy no less a sum than $50,000,000.
I should like to review a little the history of war finance in Canada, and then come back to discuss this policy. It will be recalled that in the first war budget which was brought down in September, 1939, the present Minister of Finance, then Minister of National Revenue, who delivered the war budget, laid down the broad principle of the government's policy of war finance, which was briefly the principle of "pay as you go". He elaborated that policy as consisting - of two things: (1) An initial period of quietness and hesitation. Well, there was quietness and hesitation in the government's war effort; there is no doubt
about that, and anybody who doubts it need only cast his mind back over the history of the first nine months of the war. There was quietness and hesitation not only in the government's financial effort, but in every effort of this government. Then (2) there would be a second period in which rising business activity and expanding income had acquired momentum. The minister laid down the principles which were in his judgment suitable for these two periods. I am not going to recapitulate them, save and except to say that the question of freezing wages and the question of a price ceiling on commodities was not part of the programme.
Then in the budget speech of 1940 the Minister of National Defence, then Minister of Finance, in a discussion of national income and financial policy laid down the principle that by far the greater portion of the increase of the national income should be used for war purposes, and I think we are all in agreement with that. That policy has been extended from time to time, and if I read the signs of the times aright it will be still further extended in the forthcoming budget. The Minister of Finance of that day went on to make the following statement, as reported at page 1014 of Hansard of 1940:
If an appropriate financial policy is not followed the ultimate result will inevitably be that the government will be frustrated in its attempt to procure goods for war purposes by the competition of consumers who seek to spend their increased buying power to satisfy civilian wants. In that event, also, the familiar spiral of rising prices, then rising wages and costs, and then prices rising still further would begin to work. Prices would rise more rapidly than wages and salaries, and, by this indirect, hidden and most inequitable process the civilian population, and particularly the wage and salary earners and the receivers of fixed incomes, would be forced to curtail their consumption not only of luxuries but of comforts and necessaries as well. Eventually in such a process our entire economic life would be disorganized; a hectic period characterized by feverish speculation, waste and extravagance would develop; and a collapse of the inflationary structure would be as inevitable as it was at the close of the last war.
There he was picturing the spiral of rising prices and of wages and a collapse at the end of the inflationary period. That picture is not a pretty one. It is a condition that we should seek, if possible, to avoid. But the method of avoiding that situation visualized at that time was taxation and a transfer of the buying power of the consuming public to the war effort, which is a perfectly proper method and has been resorted to in this country, in England, and in other places where this question has been uppermost in the minds of those who have these responsibilities.
War Appropriation-Finance

That was the method, one of the main methods adopted to prevent this inflationary tendency. There was always the consciousness, of course, that the old economic law of supply and demand was difficult to counteract or defeat. I have never understood that you can ever beat the law of supply and demand even if you have 100 per cent cooperation of the public. There is such a thing as scarcity and there is such a thing as plenty; when there is scarcity and there is a buying power, inevitably there will be a rise in prices, and we have it to-day in this country. No government can control this underlying law of supply and demand except by setting up new controls day in and day out, involving regimentation of the people. Even then you cannot fully control it. That is a condition which attaches to war time, and you cannot possibly wholly escape it. I will say that you can do this, you can escape it in large measure, not so much by a system of control alone, but by a system of control plus the cooperation of the people. Without that cooperation of the people you cannot make it effective.
As I tried to indicate a moment ago, after painting that picture of inflation the then Minister of Finance said that the government's financial and economic policies had been designed to try to safeguard against that type of situation, mainly by taxation; adding that that had been evolved with the aim of avoiding unjustifiable price increases or speculative excesses. Clearly the then Minister of Finance at that date, June, 1940, visualized a period of inflation in the price of consumer goods as well as in other lines of business activity. What was his remedy then? It was, as I have said not only once but twice, taxation, and that is the orthodox manner, as I understand it, of preventing this sort of thing. That was the position which the then Minister of Finance took in June, 1940.
We now come to the opening of parliament in the fall of 1940, after the mantle of the Minister of Finance had fallen on the shoulders of my hon. friend opposite. He took part in the discussion on the debate on the address, and his speech was delivered on November 21, 1940. At pages 316 and 317 of Hansard of that ' date he was answering a speech in this chamber of the leader of the Social Credit group, who had challenged the principle upon which the government's monetary policy had been based, and if I recollect aright, had moved a subamendment reflecting upon the monetary policy of the administration. In the course of his speech the present Minister of Finance discussed the policy of the Social Credit system, and contrasted it with the government policy (a) of taxation and (b) of

borrowing, which he was defending. He also referred to the dangers of inflation and the methods of controlling inflation, dealing, as I remember from reading his speech, with the Social Credit proposals for credit restriction, universal bonusing, and other suggested monetary policies. The minister than referred, as reported at page 317 of Hansard of that date, to the method of counteracting inflation by means-
I wonder whether the leader of the opposition did not use "credit restriction" where it should be "credit expansion".
Possibly I did.
Credit restriction is so contrary to our ideas.
Maybe that is my misinterpretation of the hon. member's position. I must say that I really do not understand what his position is, and I have to give the best interpretation I can.

It is expansion.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); It is mea culpa if I do not understand him. I am not going to blame him. The minister then referred, as reported at page 317, to the method of counteracting inflation by means of pricefixing on a universal scale as being the only alternative to taxation or borrowing out of savings, which was the government's announced policy. I propose to read at some length from what the minister said at that time. He said that if price-fixing on a universal scale were adopted, it would have to be accompanied by rationing and regimentation also on a universal scale. He gave the reasons. He said it was obvious that to fix prices without limiting the amount that any one person could buy would mean that only the first comers would be served. He was right in his reasoning. Therefore there would be rationing as a corollary of price fixing. In his mind-and I agree with him-the one is the complement of the other. If that method of control were to be adopted without the corollary, the first method would fall to the ground. What was the attitude of the minister then toward the entire policy of price fixing? I am reminded of a story told of the late President Coolidge. As hon. members all know, he was a man of few words. He went to church one day; as the story goes, his wife asked him what the minister preached about, and he said: "sin". "What did he say about it?" "Well, he is against it." The minister was against price fixing on the 21st day of November, 1940; there is no doubt about that.

He has been converted since then.
Well, I do not know what has happened.
He was "against sin".

He was definitely against it, and he gave then the reasons for the faith that was in him. First, that there would have to be rationing along with price fixing, and that price fixing would fail without rationing. Price fixing of a few commodities and rationing of those few commodities was possible and would be fairly easy and need not have a very serious effect. But he said this, and I call the attention of members of this committee to this statement:
But price fixing and rationing on a general scale-
Mark you; he couples the two together; one could not succeed without the other.
-have at least two disadvantages.
I give you the minister's own words:
In the first place, this would call for bureaucratic interference in the private affairs of all Canadian citizens. . . .
And he was against that.
Perhaps I am speaking a little bit figuratively here, but generally speaking there would have to be a government spy in every grocery store. The Germans did this with some success, but the Germans are experts as spies.
These are the minister's own words, and then he proceeded:
The second objection is that-
He was dealing, hon. members will recall, with monetary theories; that was the basis of his whole statement.
-to issue quantities of money and then sterilize a large part of it by rendering it useless for buying purposes so that it will not come into competition with the money used by the government in its buying, and thereby cause prices to rise, leaves the holder of the money no better off than if he did not have it. This is equivalent to taxation or a forced loan.
I agree with the reasoning of the minister, but the hon. member for Lethbridge may not agree with it.
Hear, hear.
I expected that.
The hon. member has several things to learn yet.

Well, we all learn. The older we get, the more we know we have to learn; but for heaven's sake, if anybody is to teach us let it be
intelligent teaching, so that the man in the street can understand it. I would observe this. The older we get, the more sensible we are, and we are not apt to take up new isms and fads. At least I am not, in my old age.

That does not necessarily
indicate sense.
I want the committee to note this reference, and I want the hon. member for Lethbridge to note it.
I am listening.

I quote.
It is true that the nazis in Germany have gone nearly as far as this with their price fixing and rationing, but even they with a dictatorship and with years of experience before the war, have had to combine this price fixing with very heavy war taxation and with borrowing enormous sums at interest rates higher than we pay in Canada.
This will be found at page 287, the second column of Hansard of November 21, 1940. The minister adds this testimony against the policy of price fixing:
Furthermore, if we did succeed, by price fixing in preventing inflation resulting from the financing of the war by creating new money, we would in the end only reach the same result that we shall reach by sounder methods.
I put emphasis on the words "sounder methods", for the benefit of both the minister and the member for Lethbridge.

-we would in the end only reach the same result that we shall reach by sounder methods; for if war production is to be the same in each ease there will only be the same remainder of resources left over for civilian purposes. I am in more or less agreement with that. He is answering the hon. member for Lethbridge, but it is one argument against price fixing.

speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me, let me make clear what I was arguing. Those two things must be taken together. I was answering the hon. member for Lethbridge.
The minister can make his argument. I am putting my interpretation on his words. In part he is correct.
May I interpose for a moment-

Just a moment-
I hope we can avoid such interruptions. I object to the hon. member making a speech in my speech. I am not agreeable. If it is a question I do not mind.
Courtesy would allow me to make a statement.

I think
I am pretty courteous to most people, and I find most people courteous to me; but if the hon. member wants to make a speech while I am making my speech, I object. The minister said he was only answering one point of view. I submit that the whole reasoning of his speech was an argument against price fixing, and at times he was directing his attention against inflation by the issue of new money. That is only one feature of it, but his speech is directly against price ceilings and fixings by regimentation, and he admitted right off that you could not have stabilization unless you had the two factors-not only the ceiling but the rationing system as well. Yes, and as I am reminded, by the spy system, which is nauseating to the Canadian people. They may do it in Germany, but the Canadian people do not like it, and the minister was cognizant of that fact.

We have control.

We have control, and I am not surprised at the list of employees that this board is setting up. It is setting up a number of young lawyers all over the country and a number of inspectors, and before this system is through we may get right down to the spy system. I am like the late President of the United States-I am "agin" the method, I am opposed to the method. I am going to say something about the objective in a moment, but I should like to continue. The minister can interpret it as he likes. I read the whole speech together:
There is another, and, from a war point of view, more fundamental point. It is suggested that we should finance by issuing new money so that we can bring all useful resources into production and avoid curtailing civilian demand. But if we are really to put forth the maximum effort in the war we must not only bring all our resources into use, but, in addition, restrict as far as possible civilian use of all those resources which can be used for war.
I am in agreement with the minister, on that point and against the hon. member for Lethbridge, on that specific point.
The hon. member for Lethbridge never stood for that point.

I admit that I made a dogmatic statement, perhaps without proper premises.
What does the hon. member for Lethbridge stand for? Is there anyone in this house outside of himself who knows? Nobody knows. The minister, I think, thought he knew what he was standing for. This was a prepared speech made in answer to the hon. member for Lethbridge, and I am sure the minister thought he knew what the hon. member for Lethbridge meant. Possibly, like myself, he was mistaken. Possibly his intellect is not sufficiently developed to understand what the hon. member for Lethbridge does mean. That may be my fault; it may be the minister's fault, but that seems to be the position.
He is improving all the time anyway.

I do not know whether he is. I do not think he will make any admissions along that line.
As I emphasized in the budget speech in the first week of war, it is necessary to increase employment and production to the maximum; but that is only part of our task; we must also divert all we can from civilian to war use.
We agree with that. But we certainly shall not be doing so if we refrain from borrowing and taxation. There the minister was coming back to the orthodox method of meeting this situation. That was the declared policy of

this government. Such was the attitude of the Minister of Finance and of the government towards price fixing as a policy to control inflation on November 21, 1940; such was the fiscal policy of the government. The minister opposed the policy advocated by the Social Credit party as being wrong from every point of view, not only from the point of view of monetary inflation, but on the basis of sound reason and sound business principles. He opposed it as being odious to the habits and thoughts and ideas of freedom of the Canadian people, and it is just as odious to-day.
Does the leader of the opposition oppose price fixing?

I oppose the method. I am coming to what I propose in a moment. The minister condemned the regimentation of the people. He said that every detail of our economic life would have to be controlled by someone sitting here in Ottawa. He condemned it not only on the grounds that I have indicated but on the ground that the public policy which he advocated was sounder and better adapted to the purpose the government had in view.
That was the position of the minister and his party in the autumn of 1940. That was the position which obtained when the next budget was delivered. In the budget of 1941 we got our tremendous first dose of heavy taxation, and when we witnessed some of the largest loans ever issued by a government to the Canadian people that was a continuation of that policy.
Then, because prices began to rise, because there was a period of scarcity, the government suddenly, overnight, in the face of parliament meeting within a few days, brought into effect this policy and "froze" commodity prices on an uneven level. They have been tinkering with that level ever since.
Do prices ever get even?

Well, I think the government could have used the powers it had to put them on an even level. They could have established even prices. But what did they do? They took a given period of time, between September 15 and October 11 and froze everything at that point.
Do you not have to have some basic period in which to fix prices, or would the hon. member never fix them unless they did the impossible and became even all along the line?

I agree that you must have a base, but it does not necessarily have to be fixed overnight by order in
council. The price-ceiling level can be related back to a given period of time. That is what should have been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what was done.

I am not going to elaborate this much further; I do not want to hold up this resolution. This is the longest speech I have made on this resolution since it came before the committee. Other hon. members have spoken at length. The hon. member for Temiscouata occupied more time than any other three members of the committee-I might say any five.
Is the leader of the opposition trying to beat that record?
No; I am not, and I am not making any fulsome eulogy to constitute myself the official back-scratcher of the administration.
I have to say that I can look across at the opposition and see no one sitting there whose back is worthy of being scratched.

That is a cheap remark. That does not let the hon. member out. If he has a question to ask I am willing to answer, but, if not, he had better contain himself, because, after all, he is through as I understand.
The future will show that.

The evils following inflation I am willing to admit. It is not the principle of inflation itself that is so bad, it is the results that follow in the deflationary period. That is what I think most of us fear. That is what we experienced in 1929. The minister's party were in power at that time, but they refused to read the signs of the times. That is what this country experienced after the last war when we had not much experience regarding the matter to guide us. I have said on more than one occasion that I do not want to see the evils of inflation come upon this country. But we want some plan or system adopted. There has never been a plan.
Let us have your plan.

It is not my responsibility. It is the responsibility of the government that put this policy into force; let them produce a plan. We have a system of

hit-or-miss, hit-and-run, trial-and-error. That is what it has been all the way through. Let me give a concrete illustration.
Oh, nowl
I would not go. to the back-benchers over there to get anything, because I do not think the hon. gentleman who interrupted me has a thought in the world about the matter.
Then there are two in the house in that position.

The hon. member can speak for himself. I do not want to criticize the hon. member. If I said anything that hurt his feelings, I will take it back. I do not want to hurt anyone's feelings.
Let me give an illustration of this hit-and-run, trial-and-error system. We all know that instalment buying in times of rising wages, increasing national income, especially among the wage-earning population, rapidly develops into a very bad situation. I personally have always been against this system of instalment buying. But it has been encouraged, and it is legal. There is a way to cure it absolutely; just put an order through under the War Measures Act declaring that no conditional sale of chattels shall be legal, and you will not have any more instalment buying. The people who do the selling will not sell under those circumstances; such a sale would not be enforceable.
What happened when this ceiling was put on? Very properly, I thought, they insisted upon one-third down as the initial payment, one-third in so many months, and the other one-third in so many more months. Payments were required within three periods. If the board had adhered to that, a great many of the evils resulting from instalment buying would have been avoided. Instalment buying, of course, is inflationary; it is part and parcel of the whole inflationary system of the buying of consumer goods. If the board had adhered to that system of three payments, much of the danger and many of the improper things that go with instalment buying would have been avoided. I assumed that the order had been brought into effect after consultation with the large instalment houses. I do not know whether that was true. But one day I received a letter from three firms in my city who deal in these consumer goods and who have to compete with some of the bigger houses from upper Canada, who have branches in my city. This letter protested against a change in the system of instalment buying. Apparently we were back to the old 10 per cent initial payment on furniture. In other words the board had gone back on what I

thought was a salutary proposal; and these three firms in my city, all substantial firms, protested and asked that the situation be put back where it was before. I wrote a courteous letter to the head of the board pointing out their arguments and making them my own. I received in reply a letter which, according to my interpretation, though I may be wrong, was to the effect that I did not know what I was talking about.
Did you?

I thought I did. One should know his own limitations, and perhaps I know mine better than anyone else could know them. I thought I knew what I was talking about. Well, I gave it up. The chairman of the board was in the driver's seat; I was just a lone champion of the people. That position is maintained to-day. I could go on and illustrate it in a dozen different spheres. There are constant changes of rules and policies; and I say to the minister that this programme cannot be 100 per cent complete unless, in addition to the freezing of prices, we also have the rationing method. I am not going to oppose the policy; the objective I have always thought was good, but I am dead against the method adopted.
Before I sit down I should like to say this. Here we have $50,000,000 in subsidies, which may be only a starter. That is a very substantial sum of money to be taken out of the people by taxation. This is not fiat money, I would have the hon. member for Lethbridge understand. This is not printing press money. This is real, good, hard cash paid by the taxpayers of Canada, and it is going to be paid to certain persons. In due course the minister will tell us what the proposals are.

To-night I was most interested in the attitude of the leader of the opposition. He placed himself, if not his party, unequivocally against the price-ceiling policy of the Dominion of Canada.

The
methods adopted; I was careful to distinguish between objectives and methods. You cannot put words in my mouth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Am I wrong about that? I think that is correct.

The leader of the opposition said something about a speech I made in 1940, and he made a very good argument, on the face of it, for the proposition that I have changed my mind. Well, if I have changed my mind, that is not a very great crime. No; it is not a very great crime.

It shows you have a
mind to change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But I do want to point out exactly what I was arguing on that occasion. The hon. member for Lethbridge, as the leader of the Social Credit party, had introduced an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. His amendment was in these words:
And this house further regrets the failure of the government to adopt a monetary policy that would permit a maximum war effort without either increasing debt or reducing the standards of living below that necessary for maintaining maximum efficiency;
Furthermore this house is of the opinion that a continuation of the present financial policy will further destroy the precious liberties so essential to, and recognized as being inherent in a true democracy.
And in part of his speech, he said:
Social Credit proposes to use the national credit to provide money without additional debt, without additional taxation.
I interpreted that to mean-and I think it could mean only this-that be would have financed our war expenditures, which that year were estimated to be one billion dollars- this year they will be three billion dollars or more, but that year they were only one billion dollars-not by borrowing, not by taxation, but by the creation of new money. I interpreted his speech in that way. That is how I interpreted it, and that is what he said. I argued that if we' were to issue a billion dollars of new money or credit with the Bank of Canada, or to issue Bank of Canada notes, that we would have wild inflation. I said that nothing in the world could stop inflation under those circumstances. In considering the remedies which the hon. member himself had proposed, I pointed out that one of the remedies was price fixing-universal price fixing. It was in that connection, in connection with price fixing under those circumstances, and not under present circumstances at all, when we are taxing and when we are borrowing to a terrific level, that I said that you could not have these conditions. If the hon. member will read my speech particularly in that situation, and in the light of those facts, he will find that an entirely different complexion will be put upon it.
I say that if we were now to try to finance this war, not by borrowing $150,000,000 a month, as we shall probably have to do, not

War Appropriation-Finance
by taxing to the extent of seventeen or eighteen hundred million a year, as we shall probably have to do, but by placing three billions of money to our credit in the Bank of Canada, or by the issue of that much money in notes, so that everybody in the country would have a great big bank account, or their pockets full of money, and if then we were to try to enforce a price ceiling to keep prices down-I say we would not do it without a spy in every groceiy store, a spy on every corner. It would be impossible to do it, because of the pressure of purchasing power, and prices would be terrific.
It is for this reason that we have taken, not one method to prevent inflation, but two methods to prevent inflation. During the first year or two of the war we resorted to both remedies. We tried to relieve the pressure on prices by taxation and borrowing. In the summer of 1941 the price level was jumping from one to two points a month. It was going up so much that every month I was almost afraid to look at the cost of living index. It was terrifying to see how that cost of living index was jumping. That showed that our fiscal remedies were not sufficient. The only kind of fiscal remedy which would be sufficient would be the kind they resorted to in the middle ages, when they went into people's houses and searched their mattresses and their cellars and took nearly all the money they had. You cannot do that in a democracy. You cannot impose taxes so heavy that a great many people will not accumulate money. You cannot pile them on sufficiently so that people will not still have left a lot of purchasing power, and so you have to supplement your financial remedies with direct control. Therefore we instituted the price-fixing system.
What I was arguing against in that speech was against price fixing alone. But with the two lines of approach, marching against inflation on two fronts, we can beat inflation- if we do not tear the effort to pieces, if we do not bring up small individual cases, if we do not have to listen sympathetically to every person who says, "I could make more money if it were not for this price-fixing policy." If you are going to sympathize with everybody who has a complaint and at the same time attack the policy of the government, never advancing any alternative policy, you are not helping much. Bear in mind that our policy has worked and has been copied by the' greatest democracy in the world. We are taking a course which we believe will prevent inflation. Eon. gentlemen may say: 44561-195J
"Give them enough rope and they will hang themselves," so that my hon. friends will, then be in a position later on to say: "I told you so."
I said that the law of supply and demand could not be defeated, that it was all a matter of scarcity. My hon. friend may think that is going to happen. It may happen. But I have been amazed at the success of this policy so far. It has succeeded so far. Compare conditions to-day with conditions in the last war, when we were spending on the war only 10 per cent of our national income as compared with 40 per cent to-day and when there was, therefore, far less severe pressure on prices than there is to-day. When one compares the two periods and what took place in the last war, I am confident that this is immeasurably the better policy.
The leader of the opposition said something about subsidies and that I would have to justify the payment of this $50,000,000. About a week ago I made a speech forty or fifty or sixty minutes long on subsidies, a most carefully prepared speech, in which I argued the whole matter out. I said that the total might not be limited to $50,000,000 but might be much higher, and I gave facts and figures which I think are sufficient to show that the expenditure of that money is a good investment. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) interjected at the time, "an insurance premium," and I said, "exactly," -an insurance premium against evils which otherwise would overtake us. I am not going to say anything more to-night. I am going to listen to others if they have anything to say. I do not think the burden is on me to justify this policy any further.

I am not going to take up the time of the committee in going over the past policy of the Minister of Finance and his party. I believe that every hon. member of this house is agreed that the Minister of Finance is doing a very good job in a very difficult time, and there is no reason why any hon. member, no matter which side of the house he is on, should not make that statement. It is a plain statement of fact, but again that is no reason why we should not criticize the minister on points where we feel there is room for criticism. After all, criticism must of necessity be a matter of difference of opinion.
It is a rather strange trick of fate that the advocates of laissez-faire should have been put into the position where they have been compelled to use controls to meet a crisis. We were in a crisis in this country from 1930
War Appropriation-Finance

to 1939, a crisis in which hundreds of thousands, almost millions, of the people of Canada were starving.
No.
That is not true, and you know it.

It is true, and if my hon. friend does not know it he ought to know it, because in 1936, 1937 and 1938 he was in control of the slave camps in British Columbia where the unemployed were congregated. There were at one time in that period 1,500,000 people on relief in Canada. Will anyone tell me that people on relief are not starving? They are not starving outright so that they drop on their feet, but over a period of time they die of malnutrition. Everyone knows that.
That is not fair. Point to one case where a person died of malnutrition during the depression.

That question is not worthy of an answer. Does my hon. friend maintain that the allowance received by those on relief between 1930 and 1939 was sufficient to provide them with an adequate diet that would build up health?
That is not what my hon. friend said. Let us be fair.
Will my hon. friend sit down?
My hon. friend said that people in this country died of malnutrition.
I still say that.
Name a person who died of malnutrition.
They were starving.

Order. Please understand that this is a debate in the House of Commons, and hon. members should address the Chair. The hon. member for Vancouver East has the floor, and if he does not wish to allow a question he does not need to.

I have no objection to a question, Mr. Chairman, but I do not want to be interrupted by what is merely an expression of opinion which is no better than my opinion. I made a statement of fact, and anyone who disagrees with it takes the position that the relief allowance of the people of Canada during that period was sufficient to provide an adequate diet.
I did not say that.

Well, then, the hon.
member said that they were not dying of malnutrition. Read what the doctors are saying about the recruits examined for military service. I think the leader of the opposition stated that because of the poor conditions in New Brunswick during that period a large number of men were being rejected to-day for military service. Everyone knows that is true.

To-day's
Montreal Gazette says that an epidemic of malnutrition exists in Montreal.
Yes.
Everybody is not starving that looks that way.

What I was going on to say was that we could have used controls in that period just as well as now. The Minister of Finance says that he is amazed at how the people of Canada are cooperating, but the government would never allow the people of Canada to cooperate with the government at the time I mentioned. I remember listening to the Minister of Finance addressing a gathering in the depression days and his slogan was: "Retrenchment before reform." I am satisfied that when this war is over he will no more think of a return to that policy than he would to-day accept the policy of no controls advocated in 1941.
My objection to the wartime prices and trade board is that its administration is put in the hands of big business, as is every other phase of Canada's war effort, and that in my opinion it is being used to crush the small merchant. The people who have control of the board have not the slightest sympathy with the small business man. On this subject I would like to read an item from Saturday Night, a good Canadian paper, comparable anyway with the Saturday Evening Post. In its issue of April 4, 1942, after referring to how the economy of Canada was being drastically made over by Mr. Donald Gordon, it said this:
We are merely noting a tendency in our current political life and wondering where it will land us before it stops. Mr. Gordon, no doubt with the approval of the government, has adopted the principle

Note this.
-of letting industry regiment itself through the agency of top men in the various particular industries, each functioning for his own industry; and he expresses himself as being very well pleased with the results. He is no doubt animated in this decision by the desire to interfere as little as possible with the existing set-up in the industries, and so far he is probably right in thinking that the method has

War Appropriation-Finance
worked well. But it is putting too much faith in human nature to believe that it will work perfectly in every instance; and if it leads to serious trouble in certain industries and in certain aspects the government will not be able to transfer any of its responsibility to the elected representatives of the people. It will have to shoulder the whole blame itself. And there may be a lot.
In that regard I think the editor of Saturday Night is right. The statement has been made in this chamber on numerous occasions, and was made by the Prime Minister in his radio broadcasts, that this was the greatest experiment ever attempted with the will and consent of the people. But the people had nothing at all to say about instituting these controls. The first they heard about them was when they were imposed on the people by order in council which they heard through their radios. The editor of Saturday Night continues:
It must be remembered that the men in charge of Canadian industry, from whom these self-regimenters are picked, do not include any representatives of, and do not owe any responsibility to, the workers employed in those industries. They do not include any representatives of, and do not owe any responsibility to, the consuming public, but this is less serious, because the government itself may be assumed to hold at least a watching brief for that public.
He goes on to mention what parliament has to do with it:
As for the Conservative party, with its more than 40 per cent of the electorate, the C.C.F. party and the New Democracy they have as little responsibility in these matters as the pages in the House of Commons or the animals in the Toronto zoo.
That would be bad enough; but when the whole of this control, the whole of this regimentation, is placed in the hands of the top business men of this country, without any representatives of organized labour, or of the smaller business men, it can have only one end, the complete domination of the people of Canada by big business.
That is politics.

Who said "politics"? If it is politics, let it be politics. If it is politics to speak for the common people of Canada, for the working people of Canada, I am proud of being accused of playing politics.
The leader of the opposition referred to the orders made with regard to instalment buying. Earlier in the session I put some questions on the order paper on this subject. They were these:
1.	On what grounds was the minimum down payment on the purchase of furniture and household goods reduced from 33J per cent to
10 per cent?
2.	Was the retail trade throughout Canada consulted before the change was made?
3.	If so, is there statistical information available to show, (a) the number of retailers favouring the minimum cash down payment of 33J per cent; (b) the number of retailers favouring the minimum cash down payment of 10 per cent; (c) the number of retailers favouring the minimum cash down payment of more than 10 per cent but less than 33J per cent?
4.	Why was the interest on deferred payments raised from 6 per cent to 9 per cent?
The answers were these, and they are most peculiar:
1.	The minimum down payment on the purchase of furniture, bed-springs and mattresses was reduced from 33J per cent to 10 per cent but no change was made in the requirement that the balance of the purchase price must be paid in full in twelve monthly instalments. The reduction in the down payment with consequent increase in monthly instalment payments was made because the former requirement had resulted in a substantial reduction in total sales.
It is my opinion that the purpose of raising the down payment to 33J per cent was to bring about a reduction in sales. Continuing the answer to question 1:
It seemed to be operating to prevent people of small incomes from furnishing their households and with particular severity in respect of newly established homes. The cost of furnishing a home represents a heavy capital expenditure which many people are unable to finance on the basis of a down payment of one-third of the total sum. In addition, the reduction in total sales reduced the operating margins of retailers and manufacturers and coincided with an increase in costs amounting to as much as 12 per cent which was being shared equally by retailers and manufacturers. The decision to reduce the down payment was made with a view to these circumstances and for an experimental period pending further investigation and reconsideration in the light of its results.
We come to the next answer:
2.	Individual retailers throughout Canada were not circularized or otherwise consulted before the change was made. The decision was made by the board after discussion with board officials administering these matters and representatives of retailers and manufacturers.
I have here excerpts from Furniture and Furnishings, February, 1942, issued in Toronto. The magazine states:
Prior to the announcement of the original order restricting credit last Thanksgiving, the Ontario Retail Furniture Dealers' Association polled its members to secure their opinion on down payments. The answers were as follows: a total of 871 per cent voted for down payments of 20 per cent or more; 72 per cent went further and proposed 25 per cent payments and 24i per cent favoured payments of at least one-third down. Only 10 per cent favoured down payments of 10 per cent.
I imagine that was the 10 per cent who were consulted, along with those administering the board.
War Appropriation-Finance

The "Retailer", a trade paper published in Vancouver, in its issue of February, 1942, goes on record to the same effect:
A questionnaire was sent out to the retail furniture dealers throughout the province, and the returns reveal that retailers are not in sympathy with such a move,-
That is, a reduction from 33J to 10 per cent. -and strongly object to the amendment having been made without the retail trade having been given any opportunity of expressing its opinion. Many retailers say that such a move is not consistent with the regulations that were drawn for the purpose of discouraging spending.
At a joint meeting held in the Georgia Hotel, Vancouver, of various classifications selling commodities on the deferred payment, it was unanimously agreed to request the wartime prices and trade board to make the minimum down payment on furniture and other articles in class 2, subect to a minimum down payment of 25 per cent.
We come now to the the answer to question No. 4:
Why was the interest on deferred payments raised from 6 per cent to 9 per cent?
The answer was:
The interest on deferred payments was not increased from 6 per cent to 9 per cent. A minimum rate of three-quarters of 1 per cent per month or 9 per cent per annum was fixed by the board as a reasonable estimate of the cost of doing instalment business.
They tell me in the first sentence that the rate was not increased from 6 per cent to 9 per cent, and in the second sentence they tell me that the "minimum rate of three-quarters of 1 per cent per month or 9 per cent per annum was fixed by the board as a reasonable estimate of the cost of doing instalment business, and primarily to ensure to the consumer a definite and reasonable spread between cash prices and time prices with a view to encouraging cash sales." They first increased minimum instalment buying to reduce sales, and when the thing they set out to do was accomplished, they reduced it in order to increase sales. Then they increased the interest rate in order to encourage cash payments. Can anyone justify or explain that sort of manipulation; far-reaching changes made, not only without consultation with the retailers, but against the wish of 75 per cent or more of the retailers; perhaps against the wish of 90 per cent of the retailers?
I have a letter from a merchant in Vancouver who sells on the instalment plan. Referring to this change, raising the minimum to 33i per cent, he says it had certain objectives:
1.	It, to a large extent, curtailed indiscriminate buying, which was the government's prime objective.
2.	It permitted smaller traders to compete with large transcontinental companies who had

previously sold on terms that the smaller trader could not possibly meet on account of his limited capital.
3.	It taught the public that in making a purchase a reasonable sum of money was necessary and only a limited space of time would be allowed for completing payment.
The writer then gives an example of the way in which the system worked after the reduction to 10 per cent:
By taking a concrete example of a very composite furniture sale of $300 under the original government terms, the buyer was obligated to pay $100 down, leaving a balance of $200 which had to be paid within twelve months, with an addition of 6 per cent, or $12 for interest. Now, for the same sale, the down payment is $30, leaving a balance of $270 to be paid in one year, with an addition of 9 per cent, or $24.30. The result is _ that the purchaser pays more than twice the interest to obtain ownership and loses his buying power for merchandise and other necessities in the same period, and the financier of the transaction receives $12.30 more in revenue.
Let me tell the minister that such things are creating lack of confidence in the minds of the people. I think it was Ernest Bevin who said: "Let doubt enter into the minds of my workers, and, my God, we have lost the war." Let doubt enter into the minds of the people, that they are being fleeced for the benefit of a few large industrialists or chain stores or department stores in this country, and we are preparing for trouble.
I was told-I do not know whether it is true or not-that another reason, that is, for lowering the minimum payment from 33J to 10 per cent, besides the one I have already stated-that is, putting the big transcontinental stores in a better position-is this. The curtailment of the sale of automobile and other metal appliances, due to war needs, had drastically reduced their sale. The sales of such commodities being reduced, the finance corporations that used to finance these purchases, corporations which had existed by lending money, found themselves in the position where they had considerable money on hand and no one to whom to lend it because people were no longer buying in that way.
Victory bonds.

You cannot get 9 per
cent on victory bonds, so that in order to enable these people to find a place where they could profitably lend their money, the sale of goods was encouraged by the reduction of the instalment payment from 33^ to 10 per cent.
I have enough material, from people who feel that they are being gypped in this way, people who feel that this government have sold them out to big business, that I could keep the committee going for days. I am not

War Appropriation[DOT]-Finance
going to do that. I thought I would bring this one glaring example to the attention of the committee and of the minister because I think something should be done to give the consumers, the common ordinary people of the country, representation on these boards.
I had a letter from Vancouver a few days ago complaining that in an outlying business part of the city, a large wholesale hardware firm was building a new retail hardware store. I wrote to the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board for an explanation of this, and as to the policy of the board, and he told me that the board had as yet no policy in the matter.
A person cannot get material to build a house without the greatest difficulty. But evidently another person can build a store where no store is needed and can stock it. Mr. Gordon also told me they were sending their representative out there, E. J. Burton, I think, of the Robert Simpson Company Limited, who would look into the matter and report. I am not so sure that any investigation Mr. Burton may make will be accepted with much confidence by the people concerned. I was in Montreal in November, and I saw people working in a big department store putting in a 8400,000 escalator system when the material used was needed for war work. An escalator at this time is about as needful as a fifth wheel on an automobile. But these people have been making so much money since the war began that they have to cover it up somewhere. That is something for the wartime prices and trade board to look into, if they are going to get the confidence and build the morale of the people of this country.

With regard to the controller of construction, that is not within the jurisdiction of the wartime prices and trade board. There is a controller of construction. He is in another department. I am not responsible. I presume, if I were, there would be some explanation for the incident the hon. member mentions. I am disposed to agree that there should not be large expenditures of that kind at a time like this if they can be avoided.
With regard to the other main points the hon. member made, first the complaint that the 33 j per cent requirement had been relaxed in the case of furniture and reduced to 10 per cent, the hon. member has picked out the only instance in the whole range of commodities where there has been any relaxation.
If that is the only one, certainly I could not take any other, could I?

speechtext:
No; I do not blame the hon. gentleman; but I want to make that clear,
otherwise the committee might think that was just representative of many relaxations, especially as my hon. friend in the latter part of his speech seemed to be building up a serious superstructure on that foundation that the war was already lost, or something of that kind.
I do not think the minister has any reason to say that.
That escalator would be installed for the saving of fuel in any event and would be a proper investment for that purpose.
We should not be thinking of profitable investments at this time.

More money for the
government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think we should be going on that basis at this time.
With regard to what the hon. member for Vancouver East said about furniture, as I say he has taken the one instance in the whole range of commodities where the requirement of a down payment of one-third was relaxed. The reason for that-it may have been a mistake-was that the board was most anxious to see that the price of furniture was held .at the level at which it was during the base period, and also to avoid paying subsidies. Costs had increased approximately 12 per cent. The board asked the retail trade to assume 6 per cent of that and the manufacturers to assume 6 per cent. The answer of one or both was that under normal conditions and volume they would be able to take the squeeze, but a reduction in the volume would increase their overhead and increase rather than decrease the necessity for margins. Whether rightly or wrongly, the board then said to them that for a temporary period the requirement would be reduced to 10 per cent and they take the squeeze of 12 per cent and divide it. I do not think there was anything sinister about that; I know there was not. It was not done in regard to any other commodity. There may be arguments against doing it, but that is the reason why it was done in that instance.
With regard to the other point, what the hon. gentleman referred to as the raising of the interest rate from one-half to three-quarters of one per cent a month, there was no such raise. The original order provided that the cash price should be lower than the time price by a reasonable amount. I am informed that the usual amount for carrying charges and interest on these instalment purchases is about one per cent a month. In this case the board fixed three-quarters of one per cent a

month as a reasonable amount to cover carrying charges and interest. What there is wrong with that I do not yet know.

If the minister will allow me, the answer is that the rate in the first place was set at 6 per cent a year. When the down payment was reduced from one-third to 10 per cent the interest rate was raised. There is no doubt about that; it is in the answer to the question that I received. I imagine that answer was formulated by the wartime prices and trade board.
